caption_hook: Tennessee has a tropical Cretaceous seabed, cedar glades on old limestone and the ancient Smokies.

layers.name: COON CREEK FORMATION
layers.hook: A tropical sea in West Tennessee
layers.what: A warm shallow sea once covered West Tennessee. Its fine mud buried clams, snails and crabs so gently that many fossils still have their original shells.
layers.bonus: Pterotrigonia thoracica, a clam from here, is Tennessee's official state fossil.

layers.name: SEWANEE CONGLOMERATE
layers.hook: Pebble beds on top of the plateau
layers.what: Rivers rushing off the rising Appalachians dropped sand and white quartz pebbles. Cemented together, this hard rock caps the Cumberland Plateau in cliffs.
layers.bonus: The University of the South sits right on the plateau's rim at Sewanee.

layers.name: LEBANON LIMESTONE
layers.what: Shells and lime mud settled on the floor of a warm sea across the Nashville area. Where the rock lies close to the surface, soil is so thin that only special glade plants survive.
layers.bonus: The Tennessee coneflower grows only in the cedar glades of Middle Tennessee.

layers.name: HOLSTON FORMATION
layers.what: Limestone laid down in a warm sea was later squeezed and baked into a hard, polishable stone. Quarried near Knoxville as Tennessee Marble, it has a pink-gray color.
layers.bonus: Tennessee pink marble clads the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C.

layers.name: OCOEE SUPERGROUP
layers.what: Thick piles of sand and mud washed into ancient basins, then were crushed and folded into mountains. Those hard rocks form the high ridges of the Great Smoky Mountains.
layers.bonus: Clingmans Dome, at 6,643 ft, is the highest point in Tennessee.
